strengths: The paper provides a very clear and mathematically sound analysis of why existing test-time guidance methods (such as DPS, ΠGDM) and naive guidance scaling fail to sample from the true Bayesian posterior.

The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) framework introduces two theoretically consistent estimators (gradient-based and gradient-free) that are guaranteed to converge to the true posterior as the number of samples increases.

The authors introduce a practical 'renoising' trick utilizing one-step models, which significantly speeds up the sampling of candidates from the stochastic posterior without running full inner diffusion loops.

The evaluation is comprehensive, spanning well-established low-dimensional Bayesian benchmark tasks, scientific inverse problems (black hole imaging), and natural image applications (super-resolution and prompt alignment).
weaknesses: The computational cost of CBG can be high, requiring many candidate samples ($K$) per diffusion step to achieve optimal performance (e.g., up to several hours or minutes of GPU runtime depending on $K$).

For high-dimensional image super-resolution, the method relies on a 'tiled' heuristic to decompose the global likelihood locally, which might not easily generalize to non-local or complex non-differentiable likelihoods.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: The paper clearly identifies and mathematically demonstrates the systematic biases and inconsistencies in existing test-time guidance methods, particularly the posterior mean approximation (DPS), the Gaussian approximation (PiGDM), and the common practice of naive gradient rescaling (tempering).

Consistent alternative estimators: The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) provides both gradient-based and gradient-free estimators that are asymptotically unbiased and guaranteed to converge to the true Bayesian posterior.

Practical acceleration techniques: To tackle the severe computational bottleneck of drawing samples from the intermediate posterior $p(x|x_t)$, the authors propose a clever 'renoising' trick using deterministic one-step models, which significantly speeds up generation.

Impressive empirical performance: CBG outperforms all test-time guidance baselines on the standard Bayesian inference benchmark (C2ST) and achieves a new state-of-the-art PSNR on the high-dimensional scientific black-hole imaging task.
weaknesses: High computational cost: Although the renoising trick speeds up the process, CBG still requires drawing $K$ candidate samples per diffusion step. For competitive performance on scientific imaging, it requires $K \geq 512$, which is significantly slower than standard guidance methods (e.g., 2.9 minutes vs. 24 seconds for DPS on a Titan RTX).

Reliance on high-quality one-step models: The efficiency of the renoising trick hinges on the availability of high-quality, pre-trained deterministic one-step or few-step models (e.g., consistency models or flow matching). If only a standard multi-step diffusion model is available, the computational complexity scales quadratically, making it highly impractical.

Perceptual quality trade-offs on natural images: On ImageNet super-resolution, while CBG leads in PSNR, it trails existing heuristic guidance methods in perceptual metrics like FID and LPIPS, as it prioritizes true posterior calibration over likelihood optimization.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the lack of proper calibration and correct posterior sampling in existing test-time diffusion guidance methods, which is critical for scientific and medical applications.

Provides a rigorous theoretical analysis, proving through Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3 that common approximations (posterior mean, posterior Gaussian) and conventional gradient scaling methods are mathematically inconsistent and fundamentally biased.

Proposes two consistent and theoretically sound estimators (gradient-based and gradient-free Calibrated Bayesian Guidance). The gradient-free REINFORCE-based formulation is highly versatile as it natively supports non-differentiable likelihoods.

Shows strong empirical validation on both a structured Bayesian inference benchmark (using the C2ST metric) and a high-dimensional physical sciences task (Black Hole Imaging), outperforming competitive baselines.
weaknesses: High computational cost: The method requires nested sampling loops to approximate the integral at each denoising step (e.g., requiring 2h40m per image on an H100 GPU for the black hole imaging task). This significantly limits its practical applicability in real-time or resource-constrained settings.

The manuscript suggests that accelerated/few-step diffusion models could resolve the computational bottleneck but does not provide empirical evidence or experiments to show the performance of CBG when combined with such fast samplers.

On the high-dimensional black hole imaging task, the quantitative performance gains (PSNR) over the strongest baseline (PnP-DM) are marginal (26.10 vs 26.07), although the qualitative reconstructions look highly promising.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: The paper clearly identifies and mathematically proves the inconsistency and bias in existing test-time guidance methods (Theorems 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3).
Principled solution: The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) provides consistent estimators for sampling from the true Bayesian posterior, addressing a critical gap in the literature.

Comprehensive evaluation: The authors validate their method on a standard Bayesian inference benchmark using the Classifier 2-Sample Test (C2ST) metric and demonstrate that, unlike existing baselines, CBG successfully converges to the ground-truth posterior with more compute.

Real-world scientific relevance: Demonstrating the method on a high-dimensional scientific task (black hole imaging) highlights the practical value of calibrated posterior sampling where uncertainty quantification is critical.
Excellent writing and clarity: The paper is well-structured, mathematically rigorous, and the motivation is clear.
weaknesses: High computational cost: Drawing multiple samples ($K$) from the denoising posterior $p(x | x_t)$ at each step of the outer loop introduces a significant computational overhead, making the method less practical for real-time applications.
The gradient-based estimator requires backpropagation through the diffusion sampling process, which is highly memory-intensive and limits its scalability to very high-dimensional data.

Although the gradient-free estimator alleviates gradient computation, it still requires nested loops ($O(NM)$ complexity) and takes considerable time to generate a single image (e.g., 2h40m on an H100 as reported in the appendix).

strengths: Strong Theoretical Analysis: The paper provides rigorous mathematical proofs showing that common test-time guidance approximations (such as the posterior mean approximation in DPS and the Gaussian approximation in ΠGDM) are fundamentally biased and fail to sample from the true Bayesian posterior even with infinite compute. It also proves that the standard gradient-rescaling heuristic for tempering is mathematically incorrect.

Consistent and Unbiased Estimators: The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) framework introduces gradient-based and gradient-free estimators that are asymptotically consistent, allowing users to trade computational budget for unbiased posterior sampling.

Practical Gradient-Free Alternative: The REINFORCE-type gradient-free estimator is highly versatile because it does not require backpropagation through the likelihood function or the diffusion denoising steps, making it compatible with non-differentiable or computationally expensive reward functions.

Compelling Empirical Validation: CBG achieves near-optimal C2ST scores on a standardized Bayesian inference benchmark and matches/exceeds state-of-the-art methods in PSNR on a challenging high-dimensional black hole image reconstruction task.
weaknesses: High Computational Cost: Achieving consistency requires Monte Carlo sampling from the denoising posterior at each diffusion step. This nested sampling dramatically increases the computational runtime (e.g., requiring 2 hours and 40 minutes per image), which limits its applicability to real-time or low-compute scenarios.

Implementation Details of the Inner Loop: The explanation of how the inner loop draws samples from $p(x|x_t)$ in Section 6.2 could be made more explicit. While the paper mentions using $M$ evenly spaced diffusion steps, a concrete algorithmic breakdown of this step-reduction scheme in the main text would greatly benefit reproducibility and clarity.

Analysis of Performance vs. Hyperparameters: While Figure 3 explores the compute budget for the low-dimensional benchmark, the paper would be stronger with an ablation study on how different values of inner-loop steps $M$ and sample size $K$ affect both the image quality (PSNR) and the calibration of the high-dimensional scientific imaging task.
